body:
> Broad design reference. [Prototype #2](https://github.com/egil/gh-discussion-agent-bridge/issues/2) takes precedence for the initial build; its reduced scope and manual verification contract supersede this document for the PoC.

## Problem Statement

Teams need to discuss product questions asynchronously while keeping a shared understanding of decisions, disagreements, and open questions. Word comments become difficult to follow as conversations grow. A separate coding-agent chat also misses contributions made by other team members in GitHub.

The team wants an agent to participate directly in GitHub Discussions using its own GitHub identity. Each Discussion can contain several comment and reply threads. The agent should retain the context of that Discussion, receive new contributions without repeatedly fetching them, carry out explicit requests from team members, and show when their messages have reached it.

This specification covers a small console bridge and its container packaging. It is reusable tooling, independent of the application and product model discussed by a participating team.

## Solution

Build **GhDiscussionAgentBridge**: a small .NET console application that polls configured GitHub Discussions, maintains one persistent native Codex session per Discussion, and supplies new context directly to that session. The agent uses `gh` under a dedicated GitHub user to participate in the original conversation.

Run the bridge, Codex CLI, and GitHub CLI in a Docker container with persistent local storage. The bridge gathers and compares GitHub data deterministically; the existing agent harness handles reasoning, tools, native session history, compaction, and supported delegation. A poll with no relevant changes starts no agent work.

Team members continue using GitHub's existing interface. An explicit mention can request work, the agent account's 👀 reaction acknowledges delivery to the session, and replies and conclusions stay in the Discussion. New activity continues the session even after an answer has been accepted. Labels can convey a simple rule that all configured participants must approve a proposed conclusion.

## User Stories

1. As a team member, I want to discuss product questions asynchronously in GitHub Discussions, so that I can contribute without attending a shared meeting.
2. As a team member, I want the agent to participate through its own GitHub user, so that its contributions are distinguishable from those of people.
3. As a team member, I want one agent session to follow every comment and reply thread within a Discussion, so that related exchanges share context.
4. As a team member, I want separate Discussions to have separate agent sessions, so that unrelated topics do not become one growing conversation.
5. As an operator, I want to select which repository and Discussions are monitored, so that the agent participates only where intended.
6. As an operator, I want new Discussions matching my configured scope to be discovered, so that I do not need to create their sessions manually.
7. As a team member, I want new Discussion posts and comments to reach the agent, so that it can contribute to the current conversation.
8. As a team member, I want replies to retain their parent comment and destination, so that the agent understands which question or statement I am addressing.
9. As a team member, I want edits to reach the agent as updated content, so that corrections replace outdated assumptions.
10. As a team member, I want observed deletions to reach the agent as changes, so that removed content is not presented as current evidence.
11. As a team member, I want reaction changes to include the person, emoji, and affected post or comment, so that the agent can understand individual responses.
12. As a team member, I want label and accepted-answer changes to reach the agent, so that it knows the current discussion policy and conclusion.
13. As a team member, I want the agent to receive the complete new text already gathered by the bridge, so that it can respond without fetching the same material again.
14. As a team member, I want nearby contributions grouped into a batch, so that the agent can consider them together.
15. As a team member, I want the agent to follow the chosen grilling or wayfinding instructions, so that the session helps us clarify decisions and resolve disagreements.
16. As a team member, I want contributions attributed to their actual authors, so that a summary accurately reflects participation and differing positions.
17. As a team member, I want to mention the agent to request work, so that I can direct it from the Discussion itself.
18. As a team member, I want to request research and receive findings in the original thread, so that supporting evidence stays connected to the question.
19. As an operator, I want only configured team members to issue direct instructions, so that source material and unrelated contributors do not acquire command authority.
20. As a team member, I want repeated polls and reactions to my command to preserve a single execution of that command, so that work is not repeatedly launched.
21. As a team member, I want a 👀 reaction from the agent account after my message reaches the agent session, so that I can see that delivery succeeded.
22. As a team member, I want a receipt to represent the delivered version of my message, so that an edit is not falsely shown as already delivered.
23. As a team member, I want delivery acknowledgment to remain separate from a completed response, so that I understand what the receipt means.
24. As a team member, I want human reactions to agent comments to reach the session, so that approvals and feedback remain part of the conversation.
25. As a team member, I want a Discussion label to communicate an all-participant approval rule, so that agreement can be explicit where needed.
26. As a team member, I want approvals to concern a specific proposed conclusion, so that a thumbs-up elsewhere is not mistaken for agreement with it.
27. As a team member, I want conclusions and accepted answers to be revisited when new information arrives, so that an earlier agreement does not freeze the conversation.
28. As a team member, I want unanswered discussions to remain available for later contributions, so that participation does not depend on response timers.
29. As an operator, I want each Discussion to process one agent turn at a time, so that concurrent messages do not create conflicting writers to one session.
30. As an operator, I want different Discussions to progress independently within a configured concurrency limit, so that a busy session does not consume all available capacity.
31. As an operator, I want changes arriving during an agent turn to remain pending, so that they are handled after that turn.
32. As an operator, I want session mappings and pending work to survive restarts, so that container replacement does not lose the conversation or its backlog.
33. As an operator, I want accepted input and completed processing recorded separately, so that receipt retries do not repeat agent work.
34. As an operator, I want uncertain delivery or publication outcomes reconciled before retrying, so that recovery does not blindly duplicate work or replies.
35. As an operator, I want GitHub failures and rate limits to preserve pending work, so that a temporary outage does not discard contributions.
36. As an operator, I want harness and authentication failures to be visible, so that an inactive agent is not mistaken for a successful delivery.
37. As an operator, I want the bridge to ignore its own routine posts and receipts as wake triggers, so that the agent does not converse with itself indefinitely.
38. As an operator, I want startup context and shared discovery notes available to a new or restored session, so that it can understand current decisions after a restart or compaction.
39. As an operator, I want configurable polling and payload limits, so that I can control API activity and agent input size.
40. As an operator, I want oversized or incomplete input reported and retained, so that token limits do not silently discard a participant's contribution.
41. As an operator, I want the application to run unattended after initial authorization, so that it can be hosted continuously.
42. As an operator, I want to authorize Codex through my normal ChatGPT account, so that the bridge can use the existing CLI subscription sign-in flow.
43. As an operator, I want GitHub and Codex credentials supplied independently at runtime, so that each identity has a clear purpose.
44. As an operator, I want the container's working data isolated from the host, so that research can use the internet without exposing general host access.
45. As an operator, I want concise operational status showing pending, running, failed, and uncertain work, so that I can diagnose problems without reading native transcripts.
46. As a maintainer, I want the bridge to rely on native CLI session behavior, so that we can extend harness support without building an agent runtime.
47. As an operator, I want timestamped stdout logs correlated by Discussion, session, and batch, so that I can see what is happening as the application runs.
48. As an operator, I want retained log history with bounded disk use, so that I can look back and debug failures after a restart.

## Implementation Decisions

### Scope and ownership

- Deliver one console application and Docker packaging. Use .NET and SQLite as the concrete first implementation choices: the bridge's database is a local file on persistent storage. A JSON storage backend is not additionally required.
- Codex CLI is the first supported harness and acceptance target. Keep its process/protocol integration in a small owned adapter; Claude Code is a subsequent extension using the research already completed. There is no plugin framework or generalized workflow engine in v1.
- The bridge owns GitHub polling, complete retrieval, deterministic change detection, pending batches, session routing, delivery receipts, and recovery state. The agent owns facilitation, research, native delegation, conversation memory, reasoning, and posting through `gh`.
- Facilitation instructions and supporting context are supplied at session initialization. They should direct the agent to participate in GitHub rather than wait for answers in an interactive terminal. Existing grilling or wayfinding instructions can be supplied; the bridge does not reimplement those skills or decide product requirements itself.

### GitHub scope and change detection

- Configure the GitHub repository, the dedicated agent identity, the authorized team member identities, and an explicit monitored scope. Scope can select Discussions directly or match configured categories/labels. Do not automatically enroll every existing repository conversation merely because credentials allow access.
- Use the GitHub GraphQL API for monitoring. A direct .NET client or SDK is an implementation detail; it must support the required Discussion, comment, reply, reaction, and pagination fields. Keep `gh` installed for the agent's own operations.
- Default to a ten-second polling interval, configurable by the operator. Back off on failures and respect provider rate-limit information. The bridge remains the poller; polling itself does not invoke a model.
- Read every page needed to establish the monitored state, including older parent comments, replies, and individual reactions. A partial read is not evidence that an item was deleted. Preserve the last complete state when a page or request fails.
- Compare stable object identities, relevant content and state, and individual reaction membership. A count or parent `updatedAt` value alone is not sufficient evidence of every required change. Preserve actor attribution and distinguish additions, edits, observed removals, labels, and accepted-answer changes.
- Detect changes to human reactions on agent-authored content. Suppress wake-ups caused by the agent account's own routine posts, delivery receipts, and their resulting metadata changes. Keep those contributions available as conversation context.
- Polling describes changes observed between snapshots. Content or a reaction created and removed entirely between polls may not be observed. This limitation is acceptable for v1 and must be documented.

### One session per Discussion

- The persistent routing key is the repository's stable identity plus the GitHub Discussion node ID. All comments and reply threads in that Discussion map to one native session; separate Discussions map to separate sessions. Titles, category names, and comment-thread positions are not session keys.
- Native session IDs are allocated by the harness and stored in the mapping. The bridge does not need to manufacture a native UUID deterministically from GitHub data. Recover the existing mapping before creating a replacement session.
- A new session receives the Discussion's initial context, selected facilitation instructions, team identities, current conclusion, relevant existing conversation, and available shared discovery notes. Recreated sessions receive an explicit recovery bootstrap.
- Serialize turns per Discussion. Changes observed during a running turn are retained for the next batch. Permit bounded concurrency across Discussions. Support one active bridge instance per state store; distributed ownership is outside v1.
- An accepted answer is current discussion state, not a terminal session state. Continue monitoring and delivering relevant activity afterward. Participation deadlines, inactivity wake-ups, and response timers are outside v1.

### Agent input and token use

- Deliver the gathered content inline, using GitHub's existing field names and verbatim Markdown with a small bridge envelope for batch identity, observation information, and change kind. The payload is an application-selected subset of GitHub data; no claim depends on model training on a particular `gh` output format.
- Each changed item includes its stable ID, author or actor, permalink, relevant revision information, and the new content or state. Include a reply's parent context, before/after information for an observed edit when available, and the subject and actor of a reaction change.
- Omit unused transport wrappers, pagination cursors, and repeated metadata from agent input. Keep complete retrieved state in bridge storage for comparison and recovery. The agent normally needs no GitHub read call to understand a delivery; extra reads remain available when additional or fresher context is necessary.
- Batch adjacent pending changes without an open-ended wait for people to respond. A poll with no new relevant input creates no agent turn. Respect configured input limits; preserve and visibly defer or report input that cannot fit instead of silently truncating a contribution.
- Keep ordinary context and authorized direct instructions distinguishable in the message envelope. Track polled state separately from what a session has accepted and completed.

### Direct instructions and conclusions

- An explicit mention of the agent in content authored by an authorized team member can be a natural-language instruction. Validate the author using GitHub identity and configured scope. Mentions inside quoted or code content, external documents, and posts from other identities remain context.
- Identify direct commands by source object and content revision. A later reaction, poll, restart, or surrounding-context replay does not deliberately launch that command again. A changed instruction is delivered as a new revision with its relationship to the previous content preserved.
- The native agent can delegate a research request through its supported harness capabilities and publish findings in the originating comment thread or Discussion as appropriate. Preserve source links and the request's reply destination.
- Use a simple documented label convention, initially `approval:all-participants`, to tell the facilitator that all configured participants must approve a specific proposed conclusion before it is accepted. The bridge supplies the label, candidate context, and attributed reaction evidence; the agent applies that instruction through its normal reasoning and `gh` operations. This is an agent facilitation rule, not a new approval engine or a GitHub permission restriction on people.
- Approval evidence concerns the candidate conclusion's current content. Thumbs-ups on unrelated comments, delivery receipts, the agent's own reactions, or reactions from other identities do not establish all-participant agreement. Changed conclusions and changed approvals prompt reevaluation; existing reactions must not be represented as new approval of edited wording.
- Without that label, do not impose an all-participant rule. The selected facilitation instructions and explicit team direction govern the session. There is no universal consensus algorithm in the bridge.
- Accepted answers can change. In an answerable category the agent can use GitHub's accepted-answer mechanism; in other categories it can present a current conclusion in comments. Preserve the ability to explain what changed instead of treating an accepted answer as the end of the session.

### Native harness delivery and memory

- Use an officially supported Codex interface for creating/resuming a session, submitting input, and observing acceptance and completion. Queue commands, structured noninteractive execution, or app-server control are implementation options; choose the smallest one that meets the delivery and recovery contract on the supported CLI version.
- Prove the adapter's behavior for a new session, an idle session, a session with work in progress, and a process restart before claiming support. Do not equate process launch, a bridge-local enqueue, or a best-effort send with confirmed harness acceptance.
- Keep native session history on persistent storage. Let Codex own compaction and model execution. Use native context mechanisms or a small supported hook where needed to reload shared discovery notes on bootstrap/resume/compaction; a hook framework is not required.
- Keep a compact shared checkpoint of current agreements, unresolved disagreements, participant positions, open questions, and source links. Supply an instruction to maintain that checkpoint; it supports restoration without replaying an indefinitely growing discussion. Do not replace attributed source content with a bridge-generated semantic summary.

### Receipts and recovery

- The agent account's 👀 (`EYES`) reaction means the harness accepted the corresponding message content for processing. It is a delivery receipt, not evidence of a completed response or agreement with the message.
- The bridge adds receipts after confirmed native input acceptance. Save enough state to associate accepted batches with source content revisions. Do not add a receipt for an updated revision merely because an older revision was accepted.
- When a message edit is observed, remove the old receipt until the updated content is accepted. Receipt additions/removals are performed by the bridge without an agent turn or agent tool call.
- Persist receipt updates independently from agent delivery. If the GitHub reaction write fails, retry that write without resending an already accepted input batch. Recovery checks whether the agent account's reaction is already present before repeating an uncertain mutation.
- Persist complete observed snapshots, pending batches, native session mappings, delivery outcomes, processing state, and receipt work. Use transactions for bridge-owned transitions that must survive a crash together.
- Handle uncertain outcomes explicitly. Reconcile against available native session state or GitHub state before retrying. If acceptance or an external side effect cannot be established safely, retain an actionable uncertain state for the operator; do not blindly replay an instruction or claim an exactly-once guarantee across independent services.
- The agent is instructed to check whether a reply already exists when recovering interrupted work. The bridge does not implement a second publication path for every agent tool action. Native history and observable GitHub state provide recovery evidence; model behavior remains a distinct acceptance risk.

### Runtime and credentials

- Run unattended after initial authorization. Support the native Codex ChatGPT/device-code sign-in flow and persist its configured credential store and native history across container restarts. The normal runtime does not require a human-attached terminal.
- Supply the agent GitHub user's token at runtime for both the bridge's API calls and the agent's `gh` commands. Keep this GitHub identity separate from the Codex sign-in. Do not bake authenticated credentials into the image.
- Run unprivileged with dedicated application storage and no general host filesystem or Docker daemon socket mounts. Permit research internet access while configuring the deployment's host/private-service network boundary explicitly. Containerization does not remove the authority of supplied GitHub credentials.
- Expose concise console status for monitored Discussions, mapped sessions, pending/running/failed/uncertain work, receipt failures, and authentication problems. Preserve pending work and avoid exposing secret values in logs. Missing authorization or unsupported harness behavior must be visible instead of producing false delivery receipts.
- Emit structured, timestamped stdout logs for startup, scope selection, relevant polling outcomes, detected changes, batching, session creation/resumption, input acceptance, processing completion/failure, receipts, retries, and recovery. Include repository/Discussion identity, native session ID where known, batch ID, operation outcome, and actionable error details as appropriate. Use log levels so routine unchanged polling does not obscure important activity.
- Retain a rotating log copy on the application's persistent storage, with configurable retention or size limits. Logs remain usable after a container restart or replacement using the same volume. Keep logging local and simple; an external logging platform is not required. Do not log credentials, authorization headers, or full discussion/prompt payloads by default.

## Testing Decisions

- **Protected behaviors:** when new Discussion activity is observed, the bridge delivers the correct attributed context to that Discussion's persistent agent session; accepted input receives a truthful receipt; unchanged state and the agent's own receipts do not create new work; restarts retain pending input without deliberately duplicating accepted commands.
- **Approved observation seam:** exercise the bridge through the same application-host lifecycle and configuration used by the console entry point. Keep the real application composition and real on-disk SQLite state. Replace GitHub and the native agent only at their external HTTP/process boundaries, and control time where needed for deterministic polling. Observe emitted input batches, outbound GitHub mutations, public status, and behavior after reopening the same state store. Do not introduce public test-only APIs or one mocked interface per internal class. The user approved this boundary together with a small real GitHub/Codex/container compatibility smoke test.
- **Risk and sufficient evidence:** use focused application integration tests for routing, payloads, pending work, receipt ordering, and restart behavior, because the risk crosses orchestration, serialization, and durable state. Add narrow deterministic tests only where substantial comparison or command-classification rules need cases that would be costly to enumerate through the host. Avoid repeating the same assertions across layers.
- **Boundary fidelity:** use real persistence for transaction and recovery evidence. A fake GitHub endpoint and a controllable harness endpoint make failure windows deterministic, but do not prove compatibility with either provider. Publicly observable delivery counts are meaningful where absence of duplicate command execution is the requirement; internal collaborator call counts are not the contract.
- **Core scenarios:** new root content and replies map to one session per Discussion; different Discussions remain isolated; a reply beyond the first page is included with its parent; a failed later page does not generate false deletion events; replacing one person's reaction with another's is detected even when the total count is unchanged; edits carry revised content and invalidate the prior receipt.
- **Delivery and recovery scenarios:** repeated unchanged polls produce no native input; changes during a running turn become the next batch; harness rejection produces no receipt; a failed receipt write retries independently; the bridge's own receipt produces no wake-up; a human reaction to an agent reply does; an old revision's late acknowledgment does not mark a newer edit as delivered; restarting after acceptance or an ambiguous send does not blindly relaunch the command.
- **Operational evidence:** a failed delivery or receipt exposes the affected Discussion/session/batch and the retry or uncertain outcome through captured stdout and retained logs; reopening the persistent storage preserves log history and configured rotation bounds disk use. Assert useful events and correlation fields rather than exact log prose. Check that configured credential values and routine full input payloads are absent from default output.
- **Instruction and facilitation scenarios:** authorized explicit mentions are distinguishable from quoted mentions and untrusted context; a reaction to a previously delivered command does not execute it again; the complete configured participant identities, approval label, candidate context, and individual reactions reach the session; changing an accepted answer or receiving new messages continues the same session. Deterministic bridge tests assert supplied policy and evidence, not a canned fake model's ability to judge consensus.
- **Compatibility evidence:** run small adapter checks against a disposable GitHub Discussion and the supported real Codex CLI. Verify the actual bridge adapter's authentication, pagination, reaction mutation, input acceptance, idle/active delivery, and session resumption. Use the installed provider rather than reproducing it in a permanent mock. These checks are scoped, credentialed evidence rather than requirements for every fast local test.
- **Deployed acceptance:** one bounded Docker journey demonstrates authorization, a team contribution, context delivery, a receipt under the agent identity, an agent reply in the correct thread, and continuation after restart. Inspect an all-participant conclusion round for faithful attribution and the declared policy. This assesses the assembled bridge and prompt integration; it does not guarantee all future model reasoning.
- **Meaningful red:** a behavior test must fail for the relevant false observation, such as delivering a duplicate command, publishing a receipt before acceptance, losing a pending reply after restart, or routing two Discussions into one session. During implementation, demonstrate that the introduced behavior or a deliberate reversal of its guard changes that observation. Compilation failures and missing infrastructure are not meaningful behavioral evidence.
- **Prior art and constraints:** the current repository contains documentation and no executable application, test suite, or established runner for this tool. Choose a minimal supported .NET test setup during implementation. No production code, tests, live harness messages, or Docker acceptance run have been executed for this specification.
- **Residual risks:** polling can miss transient between-poll changes; provider compatibility must be checked with the real APIs/CLI; external side effects can have ambiguous outcomes; facilitation quality and faithful application of approval instructions require bounded live acceptance and team observation. These are explicit limits rather than properties proved by fake endpoints.

## Out of Scope

- Implementation of the product features discussed by monitored teams.
- A new discussion UI, Word/SharePoint import pipeline, or repository/category reorganization.
- Agent participation deadlines, inactivity timeouts, scheduled reminders, or time-based wake-ups.
- A universal approval engine, voting DSL, forced unanimity for every Discussion, or permission changes that prevent people from using GitHub's own accepted-answer controls.
- Automatic conversion of every conclusion into ADRs, specifications, implementation tickets, or AFK code delivery. The agent may summarize and link decisions; those publication workflows remain separate.
- Claude Code and additional harness implementations in the first working version; a plugin ecosystem, custom LLM runtime, or bridge-managed compaction algorithm.
- Webhook hosting, event relays, distributed workers, multi-instance coordination, external databases, or a separate infrastructure platform.
- Perfect capture of transient activity between polls, or an exactly-once promise covering arbitrary native agent tool actions and independent remote systems.
- Provisioning a GitHub account, changing billing, or creating long-lived credentials as part of writing this specification.

## Further Notes

- **Confirmed scope decisions:** one session per GitHub Discussion, including all its comment/reply threads; new messages continue that session; accepted answers can change; no participant timers/timeouts in v1; keep the implementation small.
- **Concrete implementation choices made for a small first build:** .NET console application, local SQLite, direct GraphQL monitoring, Codex first, and a documented all-participant label instruction. JSON storage and further harnesses were considered as options, not additional required implementations. The CLI adapter's precise supported transport remains an implementation choice subject to the compatibility evidence above.
- **Test-boundary confirmation:** the user approved the whole-bridge/real-SQLite boundary with controlled GitHub/Codex endpoints and a small real GitHub/Codex/container smoke test on 19 October 2026.
- **Standalone repository:** the bridge's tracker is egil/gh-discussion-agent-bridge. Monitored Discussions belong to operator-configured repositories; the bridge is independent of any particular application.
- **Research status:** installed help and current documentation were checked for Codex CLI 0.162.0, Claude Code 2.1.300, and GitHub CLI 2.102.0. The precise wake/acceptance/restart behavior has not been tested against a live agent. Implementors must verify it rather than assume that a help entry proves the runtime contract.
- **Primary references:** [GitHub Discussion fields and operations](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/discussions), [GitHub reaction fields and operations](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/reactions), [GitHub CLI API access](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_api), [Codex CLI commands](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands), [Codex app-server lifecycle](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server), [Codex authentication](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth), [Codex hooks](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks), [Docker isolation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/).
